study.title: A new archosauriform from the Middle Triassic of southern Brazil and the early diversification of Archosauria

cover.headline: The next new species is probably **already sitting in a museum drawer**, unopened.

slides.title: A fossil lost for twenty years turned out to be a reptile nobody had ever named.
slides.body:
Collected in southern Brazil, misplaced, recovered in 2022. The team named it Silescelida acristata and placed it near Euparkeriidae.

That puts it on the branch running towards dinosaurs and crocodiles, rather than inside either one.

stat.label: years old, from the Middle Triassic

slides.title: The gap in this part of the family tree is a storage problem as much as a digging problem.
slides.body:
Dinosaurs and crocodiles share a grandparent, and that grandparent is barely known. Every specimen matters more than usual when the record is this thin.

This one spent two decades in the wrong place, and the tree stayed wrong with it.

slides.title: New species are supposed to come out of the ground, not out of the collection.
slides.body:
Fieldwork gets the photographs and the funding. Cataloguing does not.

Its legs sat halfway under the body, further in than a sprawling lizard but not upright. That stance is the shift that let archosaurs take over.

caveats: The specimen is fragmentary. Most of what survives is limb bones, not a full skeleton.
Where a species sits on the family tree often shifts once more fossils turn up.
Scientific Reports is a broad-scope journal, so this got less specialist scrutiny than a Nature paper.

caption: A reptile nobody had named spent twenty years lost in a drawer. The family tree of dinosaurs was wrong that whole time.
